paragraphs: Grushenka lived in the busiest part of town, near the cathedral square, in a small wooden lodge in the courtyard of the widow Morozov’s house. The house was a large two-story stone building, old and very ugly. The widow lived a secluded life with her two unmarried nieces, who were also elderly. She had no need to rent out her lodge. But everyone knew she had taken Grushenka in as a lodger, four years before, solely to please her kinsman, the merchant Samsonov, who was known to be the girl’s protector. It was said that the jealous old man put his “favorite” with the widow Morozov so that the old woman would keep a sharp eye on her new lodger’s conduct. But that sharp eye soon proved unnecessary. In the end the widow Morozov seldom saw Grushenka and did not bother her by watching over her in any way. It is true that four years had passed since the old man had brought the slim, delicate, shy, timid, dreamy, sad girl of eighteen from the chief town of the province, and much had happened since. Little was known of the girl’s history in town, and that little was vague. Nothing more had come to light in the last four years, even after many people had become interested in the beautiful young woman that Agrafena Alexandrovna had meanwhile grown into. There were rumors that at seventeen she had been betrayed by someone, some sort of officer, and abandoned by him immediately afterwards. The officer had gone away and later married, while Grushenka was left in poverty and disgrace. It was said, however, that although old Samsonov had lifted Grushenka out of destitution, she came from a respectable family of the clerical class, and that she was the daughter of a deacon or something of the sort.

And now, after four years, the sensitive, injured, pitiful little orphan had become a plump, rosy beauty of the Russian type, a woman of bold and determined character, proud and insolent. She had a good head for business, was acquisitive, thrifty and careful, and by fair means or foul had managed, it was said, to put together a little fortune. On one point only everyone agreed. Grushenka was not easy to approach, and apart from her aged protector, not one man could boast of her favors in those four years. This was a positive fact, for quite a few men, especially in the last two years, had tried to win those favors. All their efforts had been in vain. Some of these suitors had been forced into an undignified and even comic retreat by the firm, ironical resistance of the strong-willed young woman. It was known, too, that she had lately been given to what is called “speculation,” and had shown marked ability at it, so that many people began to say she was no better than a Jew. It was not that she lent money at interest. But it was known, for instance, that for some time past she had, in partnership with old Karamazov, actually been investing in bad debts bought for a trifle, a tenth of their nominal value, and had afterwards made ten times their value out of them.

The old widower Samsonov, a man of large fortune, was stingy and merciless. He tyrannized over his grown-up sons. But during the last year, when he had been ill and had lost the use of his swollen legs, he had fallen greatly under the influence of his protégée. At first he had kept her strictly and in humble surroundings, “on Lenten fare,” as the wits said at the time. But Grushenka had managed to free herself, while building in him a boundless belief in her fidelity. The old man, long since dead now, had had a large business in his day and was also a remarkable character, miserly and hard as flint. Grushenka’s hold on him was so strong that he could not live without her (this was especially so for the last two years). Yet he did not settle any considerable fortune on her, and would not have been moved to do so even if she had threatened to leave him. But he did give her a small sum, and even that surprised everyone when it became known.

“You’re a wench with brains,” he said to her when he gave her eight thousand roubles, “and you must look after yourself. But let me tell you that apart from your yearly allowance as before, you’ll get nothing more from me till the day I die, and I’ll leave you nothing in my will either.”

And he kept his word. He died and left everything to his sons, whom he had treated all his life as servants, along with their wives and children. Grushenka was not even mentioned in his will. All this became known afterwards. He did help Grushenka with his advice on increasing her capital, and he put business in her way.

When Fyodor Pavlovitch, who first came into contact with Grushenka over a piece of speculation, ended, to his own surprise, by falling madly in love with her, old Samsonov, gravely ill as he was, was immensely amused. It is remarkable that throughout their whole acquaintance Grushenka was completely and spontaneously open with the old man, and he seems to have been the only person in the world with whom she was. Lately, when Dmitri too had appeared on the scene with his love, the old man stopped laughing. On the contrary, he once gave Grushenka some stern and serious advice.

“If you have to choose between the two, father or son, you’d better choose the old man—as long as you make sure the old scoundrel will marry you and settle some money on you beforehand. But don’t keep on with the captain. You’ll get no good out of that.”
These were the very words of the old profligate, who already felt that his death was not far off, and who in fact died five months later.

I will note, too, in passing, that although many people in our town knew of the grotesque and monstrous rivalry between the Karamazovs, father and son, with Grushenka as its object, scarcely anyone understood what really lay behind her attitude to both of them. Even Grushenka’s two servants (after the catastrophe we will speak of later) testified in court that she received Dmitri Fyodorovitch simply out of fear, because “he threatened to murder her.” These servants were an old cook, sickly and almost deaf, who came from Grushenka’s old home, and the cook’s granddaughter, a smart young girl of twenty who did the work of a maid. Grushenka lived very economically, and her surroundings were anything but luxurious. Her lodge consisted of three rooms, furnished with mahogany furniture in the fashion of 1820, which belonged to her landlady.

It was quite dark when Rakitin and Alyosha entered her rooms, yet no lamps were lit. Grushenka was lying in her drawing-room on the big, hard, clumsy sofa with the mahogany back. The sofa was covered in shabby, ragged leather. Under her head she had two white down pillows taken from her bed. She lay stretched out motionless on her back with her hands behind her head. She was dressed as though expecting someone, in a black silk dress, with a dainty lace fichu on her head, which suited her very well. Over her shoulders was thrown a lace shawl pinned with a massive gold brooch. She certainly was expecting someone. She lay as though impatient and weary, her face rather pale, her lips and eyes hot, restlessly tapping the arm of the sofa with the tip of her right foot. The arrival of Rakitin and Alyosha caused a slight stir. From the hall they could hear Grushenka leap up from the sofa and cry out in a frightened voice, “Who’s there?” But the maid met the visitors and at once called back to her mistress.
“It’s not him, it’s nothing, just other visitors.”
“What’s going on?” muttered Rakitin, leading Alyosha into the drawing-room.

Grushenka was standing by the sofa as though still alarmed. A thick coil of her dark brown hair had slipped out of its lace covering and fallen over her right shoulder, but she did not notice it and did not put it back until she had looked at her visitors and recognized them.
“Ah, it’s you, Rakitin? You really frightened me. Who’s this you’ve brought? Who is this with you? Good heavens, you’ve brought him!” she exclaimed, recognizing Alyosha.
“Have someone bring candles!” said Rakitin, with the free-and-easy air of a very close friend who’s entitled to give orders in the house.

“Candles ... of course, candles.... Fenya, fetch him a candle.... Well, you picked a fine moment to bring him!” she exclaimed again, nodding toward Alyosha. She turned to the looking-glass and began quickly pinning up her hair with both hands. She seemed displeased.
“Haven’t I managed to please you?” asked Rakitin, almost instantly offended.

“You frightened me, Rakitin, that’s what it is.” Grushenka turned to Alyosha with a smile. “Don’t be afraid of me, my dear Alyosha. You can’t think how glad I am to see you, my unexpected visitor. But you frightened me, Rakitin. I thought it was Mitya breaking in. You see, I deceived him just now. I made him promise to believe me, and I told him a lie. I told him I was going to spend the evening with my old man, Kuzma Kuzmitch, and would be there late, counting up his money. I always spend one whole evening a week with him, going over his accounts. We lock ourselves in, and he counts on the reckoning beads while I sit and write things down in the book. I’m the only person he trusts. Mitya believes I’m there, but I came back and have been sitting locked in here, expecting some news. How did Fenya let you in? Fenya, Fenya, run out to the gate, open it and look around to see whether the captain is anywhere about! Perhaps he’s hiding and spying. I’m dreadfully frightened.”
“There’s no one there, Agrafena Alexandrovna. I’ve just looked out. I keep running to peep through the crack. I’m shaking with fear myself.”

“Are the shutters fastened, Fenya? And we must draw the curtains—that’s better!” She drew the heavy curtains herself. “He’d rush in at once if he saw a light. I’m afraid of your brother Mitya today, Alyosha.”
Grushenka spoke loudly, and though she was alarmed, she seemed very happy about something.
“Why are you so afraid of Mitya today?” asked Rakitin. “I’d have thought you weren’t timid with him. You twist him round your little finger.”

“I tell you, I’m expecting news, priceless news, so I don’t want Mitya here at all. And I feel he didn’t believe I’d stay at Kuzma Kuzmitch’s. He must be in his ambush now, behind Fyodor Pavlovitch’s, in the garden, watching for me. And if he’s there, he won’t come here, so much the better! But I really have been to Kuzma Kuzmitch’s. Mitya escorted me there. I told him I’d stay till midnight, and I asked him to be sure to come at midnight to take me home. He went away, and I sat ten minutes with Kuzma Kuzmitch and came back here again. Ugh, I was scared. I ran so as not to meet him.”
“And why are you so dressed up? What a funny cap you’ve got on!”
“How nosy you are yourself, Rakitin! I tell you, I’m expecting a message. If the message comes, I’ll fly, I’ll gallop away, and you’ll never see me again. That’s why I’m dressed up, to be ready.”
“And where are you flying to?”
“If you know too much, you’ll get old too soon.”
“Well, I never! You’re delighted ... I’ve never seen you like this before. You’re dressed as if you were going to a ball.” Rakitin looked her up and down.
“Much you know about balls.”
“And do you know much about them?”

“I’ve seen a ball. The year before last, Kuzma Kuzmitch’s son got married and I watched from the gallery. Do you think I want to be talking to you, Rakitin, while a prince like this is standing here? Such a visitor! Alyosha, my dear boy, I look at you and can’t believe my eyes. Good heavens, can you really have come to see me? To tell you the truth, I never thought of seeing you, and I never thought you’d come to see me. Though this isn’t the moment now, I’m awfully glad to see you. Sit down on the sofa, here, that’s right, my bright young moon. I really can’t take it in even now.... Eh, Rakitin, if only you’d brought him yesterday or the day before! But I’m glad as it is! Perhaps it’s better he’s come now, at such a moment, and not the day before yesterday.”

She sat down beside Alyosha on the sofa, cheerfully, looking at him with open delight. And she really was glad. She was not lying when she said so. Her eyes glowed, her lips laughed, but it was a good-hearted, merry laugh. Alyosha had not expected to see such a kind expression on her face.... He had hardly met her before yesterday. He had formed an alarming idea of her, and had been horribly distressed yesterday by the spiteful, treacherous trick she had played on Katerina Ivanovna. He was greatly surprised to find her now altogether different from what he had expected. And, crushed as he was by his own sorrow, his eyes involuntarily rested on her with attention. Her whole manner seemed changed for the better since yesterday. There was scarcely any trace of that mawkish sweetness in her speech, or of that voluptuous softness in her movements. Everything was simple and good-natured. Her gestures were quick, direct, confiding. But she was greatly excited.
“Dear me, how everything comes together today!” she chattered on. “And why I’m so glad to see you, Alyosha, I couldn’t say myself! If you asked me, I couldn’t tell you.”
“Come on, you don’t know why you’re glad?” said Rakitin, grinning. “You used to be always pestering me to bring him. You had some purpose, I suppose.”

“I had a different purpose once, but that’s over now. This isn’t the moment. Listen, I want you to have something nice. I’m so good-natured now. You sit down too, Rakitin. Why are you standing? You’ve sat down already? There’s no fear of Rakitin forgetting to look after himself. Look, Alyosha, he’s sitting there opposite us, so offended that I didn’t ask him to sit down before you. Ugh, Rakitin is such a one for taking offense!” laughed Grushenka. “Don’t be angry, Rakitin, I’m kind today. Why are you so depressed, Alyosha? Are you afraid of me?” She peeped into his eyes with merry mockery.
“He’s sad. The promotion hasn’t been given,” boomed Rakitin.
